real_case_outcomes.situation: Person in a relationship where partner communicated needs clearly and repeatedly; person acknowledged the words but did not absorb or act on them, prioritizing their own comfort and deferring change
real_case_outcomes.decision: Continued to give silence when reassurance was needed, excuses when presence was needed, and 'I'll change later' responses to immediate needs
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Partner eventually shifted from emotional distress to quiet detachment. By the time the person recognized the damage and wanted to repair it, the partner had already begun healing and had emotionally exited the relationship.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The window for repair closes when the hurt partner shifts from active distress to quiet detachment. Repeated deferral of change is not neutral — it is actively consuming the relationship's remaining trust capital.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person was harshly and suddenly broken up with by a partner who had unresolved trauma from a prior neglectful marriage and was not emotionally ready for a relationship
real_case_outcomes.decision: Went completely silent after the breakup, maintained no contact for several weeks, then gradually accepted low-intimacy contact (streaks, TikToks) while attending therapy and working on personal projects; did not frame self-improvement as proof of change for the ex
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Over several months, contact escalated organically from superficial to substantive; they reconnected and rebuilt the relationship with explicit boundary-setting and communication
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Successful reconciliation after a trauma-driven breakup required: no-contact discipline, self-investment that was genuine not performative, bilateral willingness to communicate, and incremental re-escalation of contact intimacy — not a single grand gesture

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person living in the same apartment, using the same car, in the same city as a former shared life with an ex — high environmental overlap, expected very long recovery
real_case_outcomes.decision: Stayed in the same environment but engaged actively in emotional processing rather than relocating or avoiding
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Recovered faster than expected despite the environmental overlap; the active processing work mattered more than environmental distance
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Environmental overlap is a risk factor but not determinative; active processing can compensate for inability to change environment, and relocation without processing work would not have accelerated healing

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person was told by a partner they were soulmates and 'each other's person'; partner then left for someone else within the relationship
real_case_outcomes.decision: Person attempted to hold onto the 'soulmate' framework as a way of processing the relationship's meaning
real_case_outcomes.outcome: 3 months post-breakup still experiencing acute distress; ultimately concluded that 'soulmate' and 'my person' are constructs that cause disproportionate harm when the relationship ends, and reframed compatibility as contextual and changeable rather than destined
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Deeply held romantic idealization frameworks ('the one', 'soulmate') amplify grief severity and duration when the relationship ends via betrayal; dismantling the framework — not just the relationship — is a necessary part of recovery

real_case_outcomes.situation: A nearly 3-year relationship including promise rings ended with the partner citing lost spark and no specific triggering event
real_case_outcomes.decision: The person chose to accept the ending rather than pursue repair, reframed their approach to future relationships as 'going with the flow' rather than forcing, and resolved to stop holding onto things that clearly both parties no longer wanted
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Reported a subjective sense that 'life smooths out' when accepting rather than fighting natural endings; described remaining open to future relationships while no longer placing unconditional trust in early declarations
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a partner exits citing lost feeling with no repairable triggering event, and the committing gestures (promise rings, declarations) have already proven unreliable predictors, the highest-return decision is acceptance and recalibration of future commitment signals — not repair attempts

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person in a 2.5-year relationship that included shared routines, family involvement, and near-daily contact — ended abruptly when partner stated feelings were gone, with no prior warning and no closure; partner quickly reconnected with an ex afterward
real_case_outcomes.decision: Person did not pursue the ex or attempt reconciliation but was left without a support network and struggled to re-engage with hobbies or solo activities
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Remained in a prolonged stuck state — unable to pursue previously enjoyed activities because they were emotionally associated with the ex, and unable to build new friendships due to grief-related energy depletion
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Making a partner your sole social world and planning all activities around them creates a double loss at breakup — both the person and your entire independent life framework. Recovery requires rebuilding both simultaneously, which is significantly harder than either alone.

real_case_outcomes.situation: 6-year cohabiting relationship where one partner carried all relational labor while the other gradually checked out; ended by the disengaged partner
real_case_outcomes.decision: After initial grief (months 1-4), the abandoned partner pursued full no contact, reinvested in friendships and family, pursued fitness and discipline, took solo travel, and used writing as emotional processing
real_case_outcomes.outcome: By months 7-10, the person reports a reconstructed identity, stronger social connections than during the relationship, and a sense of aliveness described as new
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Relationships where effort was severely asymmetric often mask a slow erosion of the carrying partner's individual life; the breakup, though painful, can restore what was lost in that erosion

real_case_outcomes.situation: 4.5-year relationship ended mutually; both parties acknowledged growing apart and having different visions for the future; no toxicity; strong emotional connection and compatibility in most areas
real_case_outcomes.decision: Agreed to separate despite the relationship being 'healthy and something out of a dream'
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Poster reported simultaneous grief and relief — a mixed emotional state that confirmed the decision was right even though it was painful
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The presence of relief alongside grief is diagnostic — it signals that the relationship was already creating a burden the person hadn't fully named; a clean ending from a good relationship is still an ending and produces real grief

real_case_outcomes.situation: Relationship ended because of jealousy and clinginess around the partner's opposite-sex friendships; ex blocked OP on all platforms after repeated contact attempts
real_case_outcomes.decision: Entered genuine no-contact, started therapy for jealousy, rebuilt social life, dated others, and stopped orienting daily life around the ex
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Ex reached out after three months; reconciliation happened two months later on the ex's initiation; OP reports jealousy is resolved and relationship is proceeding slowly
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Behavioral change that is visible and durable — not just promised — can reopen a closed door; however, the story also carries a dissenting signal from multiple commenters who noted the timing and 'guy friends' framing suggests a third party may have been involved, meaning the outcome may be less stable than it appears

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person in a 3.5-year marriage with an avoidant partner shaped by a traumatic father figure; both partners struggled with mental health; arguments were chronic
real_case_outcomes.decision: Initiated divorce himself, despite still loving his wife
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Experienced ongoing regret, loneliness, and grief post-divorce; while hospitalized, realized that romantic interest from new women did not substitute for his ex-wife; concluded the real work was addressing pre-relationship trauma, not replacing the person
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Initiating a breakup does not resolve attachment or grief; if the root cause is intergenerational trauma absorbed before the relationship began, leaving the relationship does not fix it — therapy and deliberate solo healing are required regardless of who ended it

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person in a 7-year relationship, 7 weeks post-breakup, compiling recovery insights from extensive reading and listening
real_case_outcomes.decision: Synthesized community wisdom into an actionable framework and shared it publicly as a way of processing and giving back
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Framework received engagement and validation from multiple commenters identifying with specific elements (attachment theory section particularly resonated); became a reference post
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Structuring and externalizing what you are learning during grief (writing, compiling, sharing) can itself be a processing mechanism — it creates distance from the raw emotion and gives the experience meaning

real_case_outcomes.situation: 21F in a 6-month relationship where partner accelerated intimacy rapidly (early 'I love you,' emotional enmeshment, marriage jokes). Partner broke up on their anniversary citing religious guilt and incompatibility of faith, cried, said he still cared. Suggested she convert 'by name only' as a condition to continue.
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP respected the stated reason, did not push back, spent a month attempting to heal around the religious incompatibility narrative. Later discovered ex was on Bumble with a 'not looking for anything serious' casual profile.
real_case_outcomes.outcome: OP realized the religious reason was fabricated; actual motivation was wanting to return to casual dating. The month of processing had been built around a false premise. OP expressed anger at the deception but also reported eventually rebuilding through new friendships and hobbies.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a partner's post-breakup behavior directly contradicts their stated reason, the stated reason should be retroactively discarded. Recovery built on a false narrative is not wasted — it still produces healing — but reframing around the deception (rather than the stated incompatibility) is necessary for accurate self-understanding.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person in a 9-year relationship repeatedly tried to initiate repair conversations; partner consistently refused to engage or communicate meaningfully
real_case_outcomes.decision: On the final night, gave the partner an explicit opportunity to say anything — partner remained silent; the person then ended contact
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Relationship ended; person reported processing the ending through reframing the partner's silence as a definitive answer about what the partner was capable of giving
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Sustained silence in the face of explicit, low-barrier invitations to engage is itself a complete answer about a partner's willingness — waiting longer does not change the answer

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person was deeply in love with someone for years; relationship ended
real_case_outcomes.decision: Eventually accepted finality, removed ex from social media, stopped monitoring their profiles, and acknowledged that the only real thing they had in common was each other
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Feelings faded over time; person reached a state where they could look back without active grief and recognized the relationship's structural insufficiency
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Acceptance of permanent closure — not just distance or time — is the active mechanism that enables emotional recovery; and 'having each other' as the primary commonality is not a sufficient relational foundation

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person raised by grandparents as their child; biological mother (presented as sister) was hostile and eventually cut off; person learned the truth at age 19 when the biological mother confirmed it hostilely and told them to kill themselves
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP is processing the revelation, maintaining existing relational labels (grandparents as parents, aunts/uncles as siblings), and trying to understand whether the biological mother's hostility reflects something that happened to her
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Significant psychological destabilization; fear of using accurate biological labels; uncertainty about whether to feel angry at caregivers for the deception; extended family relationships becoming strained
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When secret parentage is revealed in adulthood via a hostile confrontation rather than a prepared disclosure, the person simultaneously loses their coherent family narrative and receives a rejection — the double wound is significantly harder to process than either alone would have been

real_case_outcomes.situation: A pregnant woman gave birth unexpectedly in her close friend's husband's car. The friend went silent; the husband sent a hostile message about the car; the friend eventually blocked OP after OP sent multiple sincere apology and payment-offer messages.
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP continued direct outreach, escalating sincerity and specificity of payment offers, before eventually deciding to try routing through a mutual friend
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Friend deleted and blocked OP. Multiple commenters with experience of abusive relationships identified the pattern as consistent with a friend in a coercive relationship protecting both herself and OP — not a genuine friendship rupture.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a partner intercepts a friendship dispute and the friend's behavior becomes constrained and erratic, the friendship repair process must be paused and the friend's safety assessed first. Direct outreach in this context can worsen the friend's situation rather than resolve the conflict.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Woman discovers her long-term partner (5 years) has a post on a 'are we dating the same guy' page. She posts anonymously, gets corroboration from another woman that he made identical exclusivity promises. He comes home furious, slams doors, refuses to speak. The other woman deletes her responses at his apparent instruction.
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP remained in the shared apartment, did not confront directly, and asked the community whether to wait for him to speak first.
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Evidence was deleted before OP could document it. Partner reframed himself as the wronged party (his privacy was violated). OP is left with no corroboration, a hostile cohabitant, and a passive posture.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: In infidelity discovery situations, delay and passivity consistently benefit the partner who cheated. The window to document, confront on your terms, and secure your position is short and closes fast once the partner knows you know.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Adult child's mother repeatedly sent cruel, manipulative messages to the partner behind the child's back for an extended period; partner absorbed the harassment silently to avoid causing conflict
real_case_outcomes.decision: Partner confided in a friend rather than the SO; SO discovered by accident via phone
real_case_outcomes.outcome: SO now faces the decision of how to act; partner has been carrying psychological harm alone for an unknown duration; relationship safety is compromised
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Silence about ongoing third-party interference does not protect the relationship — it creates a secondary rupture when the secret-keeping is discovered, on top of the original harm

real_case_outcomes.situation: 22-year-old woman on oral contraceptives using a pill organizer discovers her boyfriend replaced active pills with sugar pills from retained blister packs, resulting in pregnancy. Boyfriend's mother had been consistently pushing pregnancy themes. Relationship already strained by incompatibility and partner's lack of accountability.
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP left the shared apartment to stay with parents, confided in a mutual friend who elicited a text admission from the boyfriend, made an appointment to terminate the pregnancy, and decided to end the relationship without disclosing termination plans to the boyfriend.
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Boyfriend admitted the tampering almost immediately when prodded via text. OP confirmed termination decision based on chronic illness risk and unwillingness to co-parent with the perpetrator. Planned to file a police report using the text admission as evidence.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Physical evidence combined with a third-party text admission creates a viable path to both clean exit and police report without requiring the victim to directly confront a dangerous person. Speed of admission when indirectly approached suggests perpetrators of reproductive coercion often cannot maintain denial when given a low-stakes channel to confess.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Married woman with infant, husband had previously 'improved' after postpartum conflict, passes out unexpectedly while sick; husband leaves her on floor, goes to bed, then is angry with her the next morning
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP did not immediately act but began recognizing a pattern — recalled postpartum yelling incident, prior illness responses, and the nagging feeling she had suppressed
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Irreversible perception shift — 'I can never see him the same.' OP is at the beginning of a decision process, not an endpoint, but the psychological threshold has been crossed
real_case_outcomes.lesson: A single acute event can crystallize years of suppressed pattern recognition into a permanent shift in how a partner is perceived — this is not impulsive; it is delayed processing of accumulated evidence. The shift itself is a data point worth taking seriously rather than trying to walk back.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Partner involved police (welfare check) against someone in a way that humiliated and destabilized them, then acted loving and cuddly while waiting for police to arrive, and afterward minimized it as a mistake
real_case_outcomes.decision: Commenter described two real cases where women stayed with partners who used this exact tactic
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Both women experienced serious, lasting mental health damage — one was still recovering 10 years later, one 2 years later. The tactic escalated in both cases: one used it to make the victim feel unsafe in her own home and dependent on the abuser; the other used it as ongoing leverage and threat in future arguments
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Police-involvement as a relationship tactic — particularly when followed by minimization and affection — has a documented escalation trajectory. Treating it as a one-time mistake without hard consequences predicts worsening outcomes

real_case_outcomes.situation: 27F discovers after 7 years that her boyfriend has been telling his family and community they broke up 4 months ago, has an active Tinder profile, and was caught physically with another woman. They are registered domestic partners in California, co-tenants on a lease, and he is on her health insurance.
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP immediately begins packing with best friend, takes the dog, plans to leave before partner returns from flight, emails leasing office for early termination, completes domestic partnership termination form, emails HR to remove ex from insurance, and separates bank accounts
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Clean exit executed before partner returns; all major administrative ties identified and initiated for dissolution within hours of discovery
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a partner has been constructing a parallel exit — not just committing a discrete act of infidelity — the correct response is not 'should I try to repair this' but 'how do I execute a clean legal and logistical separation before they return.' The practical checklist (lease, insurance, domestic partnership filing, bank accounts, credit cards, pet custody, apartment documentation) is the immediate priority.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person used a close friend's spouse — an estate planning attorney's staff member — to set up a trust after receiving an inheritance; the staff member disclosed details of the estate plan to the person's ex (who shares custody of his child) over drinks
real_case_outcomes.decision: Person confronted the friend and received an apology; was asked by both the friend and the spouse not to report to her employer
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Ex is now aware of the inheritance and is making demands; co-parenting dynamic is damaged; OP is left deciding whether to report while absorbing pressure from both sides not to
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Using a personal contact for sensitive professional services creates a conflict of interest that the contact may not be able to manage — especially when that contact has a separate close relationship with someone who has adverse interests to you. The apology does not undo the structural damage to the co-parenting relationship.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person experienced significant weight loss and entered dating market; new partner made a comment revealing contemptuous attitudes toward heavier bodies ('nothing above a size 12 should exist') while not knowing they applied to her
real_case_outcomes.decision: The commenter recognized the statement as character-revealing and became more selective in dating afterward — specifically using less flattering photos on dating apps to pre-screen for appearance-conditional attraction
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Identified that many post-transformation dating options were shallower than pre-transformation options; developed filtering strategies to identify partners attracted to her beyond appearance
real_case_outcomes.lesson: After a significant appearance change, the pool of available partners expands but the quality of character within that pool does not — active filtering for appearance-conditional vs. character-based attraction becomes necessary

real_case_outcomes.situation: OP's close friend distanced and blocked her after an accidental emergency birth in the friend's car. The friend's husband was hostile and actively stoked the friend's resentment. OP and wife paid for all car repairs before attempting reconciliation.
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP waited, allowed silence to create space, ensured material restitution was complete, and accepted the friend's unexpected visit without defensiveness — mutual apology followed.
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Friendship repaired; friend acknowledged she had not actually been angry at OP but at the situation, and that her husband had convinced her to feel otherwise. Friend asked husband to stop bringing it up. Relationship restored though acknowledged as needing gradual rebuilding given husband's continued hostility.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a friendship rupture is driven by a third party's influence rather than the friend's genuine feelings, space and completed restitution can allow the friend to locate their own emotions — making direct reconciliation possible once the partner's framing loses its hold. The repair does not require defeating the third party; it requires outlasting their acute influence.

real_case_outcomes.situation: 30F, childfree, pregnant; fiancé (32M) who had agreed to be childfree expressed excitement about the pregnancy; OP suspected he might have just been performing excitement to match what he thought she wanted
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP asked directly whether his excitement was genuine or performed, then stated clearly she was getting an abortion and that the relationship was over if he had changed his mind about being childfree
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Fiancé confirmed genuine desire for a child; became coercive and refused to accept her decision; OP left the home that night, stayed with a friend, retrieved documents and essentials, and proceeded with abortion planning; relationship ended
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a partner's stated core value (childfree) shifts after a triggering event, the only reliable diagnostic is a direct binary question followed by observation of whether they accept your autonomous decision — not their verbal answer alone

real_case_outcomes.situation: 24-year-old woman with infant, husband with escalating controlling behavior (neglect during illness, emotional dismissal, rage episodes), isolated support network, mother-in-law aligned with husband
real_case_outcomes.decision: After strangulation incident, called police, obtained temporary restraining order, moved herself and child to grandmother's home, removed belongings from shared apartment, attended court hearing
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Physical safety achieved in short term; husband at his mother's; legal process initiated; OP processing acute trauma while managing child's questions about absent father
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The decision to call police was attributed partly to having disclosed publicly beforehand — external accountability (even anonymous community support) provided the activation energy to take protective action that the person might not have taken in isolation; social disclosure before a crisis can function as a commitment device

real_case_outcomes.situation: 27F discovers boyfriend of 7 years has been on Tinder and in a parallel relationship for at least 4 months; they were actively planning a wedding; he was abroad when she discovered it
real_case_outcomes.decision: Left before he returned: cancelled shared utilities, packed belongings, documented the apartment on video, emailed leasing office, terminated domestic partnership, updated all financial and insurance records, blocked him and his family on all channels
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Clean physical and digital departure completed before his return; his family contacted her with initial hostility but softened when she provided timeline evidence; cheater's email contained no apology; OP was safe at a friend's house with practical separation complete
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Acting during the window before the cheater returns — when you have logistical control and they cannot exert direct pressure — is the highest-leverage moment in a departure; completing the administrative checklist in that window produces a cleaner separation than any confrontation would

real_case_outcomes.situation: Married father with young daughter; wife progressively radicalized into conspiracy theories and online hate communities; OP had been avoiding confrontation and hoping for improvement
real_case_outcomes.decision: Following community advice: documented neglect and behavior, audited joint accounts, consulted a divorce lawyer; upon confrontation about financial withdrawals, wife became violent; OP left, police were called, wife was arrested; OP applied for and received a DV restraining order and temporary sole custody
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Divorce proceedings underway with lawyer assessing strong case for sole custody; wife has supervised visitation only; facing misdemeanor domestic battery charge; wife's own family is supporting OP
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Acting on legal and financial advice before confrontation, combined with the documented DV incident, converted a difficult custody battle into a strong legal position — delay had already cost significant joint savings but earlier action would have limited the financial damage

real_case_outcomes.situation: 34F in a serious 1.5-year live-in relationship discussing marriage; spent $400 on partner's gift after explicitly signaling it three times; partner gave nothing on Christmas morning, then retroactively claimed a pre-trip sweater was the gift; same non-gifting pattern occurred the prior Christmas
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP held composure during the family event, broke down privately, accepted partner's reactive apology hug, and began reconsidering the relationship
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Commenters broadly validated the reconsideration, with multiple independently flagging the children's exclusion as the more serious signal; no resolution reported in the thread
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a behavioral failure is (a) a second occurrence, (b) accompanied by a dishonest cover story, and (c) extends to the children not just the adult partner, the individual incident is diagnostic of a broader investment and integrity gap — not a correctable miscommunication

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person experienced traumatic loss (father to suicide at age 26) during a marriage; grief consumed nearly all relational headspace for approximately four years
real_case_outcomes.decision: Continued in the marriage with couples therapy; did not leave despite coming close to divorce
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Couples therapy saved the relationship; marriage survived, but it required approximately four years of impaired relational functioning before recovery began
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Traumatic parental loss can consume relational capacity for years rather than months; couples therapy is a meaningful intervention but requires real engagement; the healthy partner must be prepared for a multi-year timeline

real_case_outcomes.situation: Pregnant woman, married 5 years with a toddler, discovers her husband has maintained a padlocked room for 6 months with a key she cannot access; confronts him, is met with defensiveness, gaslighting (pregnancy hormones framing), refusal to open the door, and then a staged reveal the following morning
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP is considering separation but has not yet decided; posted seeking validation of whether the concern is reasonable
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Not yet resolved at time of scraping; multiple commenters confirmed the behavioral pattern (gaslighting, staged reveal, framing her as controlling) is serious regardless of what was in the room
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The tactics used to protect a secret — not just the secret itself — are relationship-defining data; a partner who will gaslight, isolate, and stage evidence under pressure over something 'minor' has revealed their conflict behavior pattern

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person with known memory difficulties bought a rare, thoughtful gift two months early, hid it securely, forgot the location on the anniversary, and covered with a false shipping delay story
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP is weighing whether to continue the search in secret for one week or disclose immediately
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Community consensus (corroborated across multiple comments) was to disclose immediately — the partner had already shown understanding, the lie is still young and forgivable, and disclosure enables collaborative search
real_case_outcomes.lesson: A cover story converts a forgivable logistical failure into a trust question; disclosing before the deadline is discovered preserves relational safety and reframes the incident as endearing rather than deceptive

real_case_outcomes.situation: 32F married 5 years (together 9-10), three children, CPTSD history, husband (38M) with past addiction (8 years sober). Multiple friends independently express concern about husband's dismissive and controlling behavior in group settings. OP does not fully register behavior in real time. Currently in couples and individual counseling.
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP brought the friend's feedback into individual therapy session without showing the post; therapist independently agreed with community observations and helped OP develop boundaries to raise in couples counseling
real_case_outcomes.outcome: OP reported therapist's independent validation aligned with community feedback, reducing self-doubt somewhat — ongoing, no resolution yet reported
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When you have CPTSD or trauma-based self-doubt, having your individual therapist independently evaluate the same behavioral evidence (without showing them community feedback) is a high-value calibration step — convergent assessment from therapist and outside observers is stronger than either alone

real_case_outcomes.situation: Husband in an apparently functioning long-term marriage came out as polyamorous, immediately had a specific neighborhood woman lined up, refused all limits, blocked partner's equivalent freedom, agreed to cut contact then covertly continued it with deleted messages
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP remained in the relationship, attempted to accommodate, stopped pursuing her own connections to protect his mental health, absorbed all household and financial labor while spiraling
real_case_outcomes.outcome: OP is barely functioning, finances deteriorating, physical and mental health declining, has fully internalized partner's framing that her reactions are the cause of the problem
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Staying in a relationship where you absorb all costs while receiving no reciprocal accommodation and are repeatedly deceived does not produce stability — it produces progressive functional collapse; the decision to stay must be evaluated against this trajectory, not against the best-case scenario

real_case_outcomes.situation: A formerly highly independent woman (solo travel to 30+ countries, self-sufficient from young adulthood) entered a relationship where her younger boyfriend took over transportation, cooking, cleaning, laundry, and trip planning. She accepted this over several years.
real_case_outcomes.decision: She allowed the dynamic to continue without actively maintaining any household responsibilities, partly because it felt like receiving the parental care she had been denied in childhood
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Within a few years she found basic chores stressful and exhausting when alone; she identified that she had lost the independent self she previously had and felt identity dissonance despite material comfort
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Functional independence is a maintained skill, not a permanent trait — even highly capable people can lose practical competence through sustained non-use, and the loss is invisible until the support structure is temporarily removed

real_case_outcomes.situation: A person going through post-surgical recovery had a partner who was emotionally absent, complained about their own minor pain during recovery, and caused chronic household stress
real_case_outcomes.decision: Left the relationship and entered a subsequent relationship with a partner who provided genuine mutual care
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Commenter reported that the new relationship demonstrated what healthy partnership actually looks like — bidirectional care even when both parties are 'chronically broken'. The contrast made the dysfunction of the first relationship legible.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: You cannot accurately evaluate whether your current relationship is abusive or dysfunctional if you have never experienced a functional one. Exposure to a genuinely supportive partnership recalibrates the baseline and makes the prior harm visible in retrospect.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Woman married one year, together four years; husband has untreated Retroactive Jealousy OCD that has driven virtually every conflict in the relationship; husband threatens divorce after she requests space following an anniversary conflict
real_case_outcomes.decision: Rather than capitulating to the divorce threat, she held her boundary, told him she would not continue to accept the current treatment, issued a clear ultimatum requiring him to seek professional help, and began building an exit plan while also opening up to her mother for support
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Husband's divorce threat was not followed through; he began engaging with a treatment plan (ERP scheduled, reading list established); OP reported feeling stronger and more self-respecting than at any point in the relationship
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Holding a firm boundary in response to a control-based divorce threat is more likely to produce genuine change than capitulation; the threat dissolves when the person being threatened demonstrates they are willing to accept the outcome the threat is designed to prevent

real_case_outcomes.situation: Man in 5-year relationship discovers partner has been in months-long emotional affair with someone else while they were jointly planning a house purchase and future together; partner disclosed before physical infidelity occurred but is leaving to pursue the new person
real_case_outcomes.decision: Partner chose to disclose and separate rather than continue concealing or attempting repair
real_case_outcomes.outcome: OP is left with extreme entanglement — partner's tattoo art on his body, partner's artwork embedded in his upcoming album, shared cats, shared life infrastructure — making routine recovery significantly harder than a less-entangled breakup
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Emotional affairs that are disclosed rather than discovered may indicate the leaving partner has already mentally exited; the disclosure is an exit notification, not a repair attempt. The depth of life-entanglement (physical, creative, financial) is an independent variable that multiplies grief complexity regardless of the emotional betrayal itself.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Woman discovers husband's affair with a coworker he had specifically reassured her about; the relationship had pre-existing covert manipulation patterns she had not named as such; no children involved
real_case_outcomes.decision: Left the marriage, moved to a new city that better matched her actual personality, pursued therapy specifically focused on understanding why she had chosen and tolerated the relationship, did not prioritize dating in the recovery period
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Five years later: owns a home, has a rich social and experiential life, describes herself as fulfilled; ex-husband and affair partner both lost their teaching jobs due to the affair being known at their school, relocated, and are reportedly socially isolated from their former friend group
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The combination of geographic change, therapy focused on selection patterns rather than just grief, and willingness to stay single rather than settle produced durable recovery; the absence of children simplified the exit and allowed complete no-contact, which appears to have been a material factor in the clean break

real_case_outcomes.situation: F22 in a 2.5-year relationship with M25 who held traditional housewife expectations and responded to her expressed hurt with defensiveness, deflection, and blame
real_case_outcomes.decision: Had one final diagnostic conversation; when partner immediately deflected and attacked her character, she did not argue, packed her belongings, left, and blocked him on all channels before he could re-engage
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Partner sent a minimizing retraction text within hours ('didn't mean it like that'); because she had already blocked him, the contact had no effect. She reported immediate and significant relief.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The decision to block before or immediately upon leaving — before the recontact cycle begins — is the structural move that makes the exit durable. Waiting to see if the apology is genuine reopens the loop.

real_case_outcomes.situation: 25-year-old leaving an 8-year relationship with a 33-year-old partner who had shown controlling and manipulative behavior; had never lived independently (went from parents' home to this partner); planned a covert exit but partner took an unexpected sick day and was home when OP woke up
real_case_outcomes.decision: Abandoned the smooth exit plan; grabbed pets and essential items immediately; sent breakup via text and blocked all channels; arranged an escort group to retrieve remaining belongings; relocated several hours away
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Safe exit achieved; belongings recovered; pets safe; no physical confrontation; partner was deterred by presence of group and left the property
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a covert exit plan is disrupted by the partner being unexpectedly present, the correct move is immediate departure with essentials rather than waiting for a better moment — and a group escort for subsequent retrieval is sufficient deterrent for non-violent but controlling partners

real_case_outcomes.situation: 21F in a relationship with 25M who issued a breakup ultimatum over a cosmetic choice (hair dyeing); OP described herself as someone who habitually gives second, third, and fourth chances
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP proceeded with the change anyway, then initiated a conversation to understand the partner's reaction rather than acting immediately on the ultimatum; when the partner continued being disrespectful and backtracked to calling it a joke, OP ended the relationship
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Breakup was easier than anticipated; OP discovered post-breakup that partner's prior long-term girlfriend had the same hair color, suggesting unresolved emotional residue was the unstated driver of the controlling behavior
real_case_outcomes.lesson: A controlling ultimatum over a minor personal choice is a reliable signal of a broader control dynamic — and the partner's behavior during the follow-up conversation (continued disrespect, backtracking, refusal to apologize) is more diagnostic than the original threat. Habitual chance-giving delays acting on already-clear signals.

real_case_outcomes.situation: 25M whose 23F girlfriend repeatedly reacted with visible disgust to his hobbies (anime, gaming-adjacent interests), causing him to feel ashamed and reluctant to share parts of himself
real_case_outcomes.decision: Had a direct, emotionally honest conversation naming the cumulative impact, not just the individual incidents — framed it as a fear of building resentment, not just a complaint about specific moments; listened to her explanation about past negative associations with people who shared those hobbies
real_case_outcomes.outcome: She acknowledged the behavior, explained its origin in past experiences rather than actual feelings about him, both parties cried and agreed to mutual mindfulness; in a subsequent low-stakes interaction she asked curious questions about his anime instead of reacting negatively
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a partner's hurtful behavior has an identifiable external origin they can articulate and distinguish from their feelings about you, a single honest conversation can shift the dynamic — but the test is consistency in subsequent low-stakes moments, not the conversation itself

real_case_outcomes.situation: 4-year relationship with recurring unresolved problems, complicated by long-distance and employment instability; couple reconciled multiple times and reached high-commitment milestone (partner met family)
real_case_outcomes.decision: Continued the relationship through cycles of breakup and reconciliation, deferring resolution of core issues; ultimately ended the relationship after long-distance finally resolved and partner gained stable employment
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Relationship ended despite the removal of the two main external stressors; 4 years of investment and a family-introduction milestone were reached before the terminal split
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Removing external stressors does not resolve accumulated unaddressed interpersonal problems; if core issues are not explicitly worked through during each reconciliation, they compound and eventually become terminal regardless of how favorable external conditions become

real_case_outcomes.situation: Woman (小林) was broken up with after frequent fighting; she initially clung and pleaded, which caused the ex to progressively reduce contact and eventually block her
real_case_outcomes.decision: Joined a support community, underwent genuine no-contact focused on career advancement rather than reconciliation tactics; re-initiated contact only when a real work need arose, without emotional agenda
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Over three months her self-confidence and career improved substantially; re-contact over a legitimate work task created a calm, non-needy interaction; the ex eventually pursued her; she declined because she had lost interest and developed better options
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The conditions that make an ex want to return (your self-possession, apparent indifference, visible life progress) are only achievable if the no-contact period is used for genuine self-reconstruction rather than tactical waiting — and by the time those conditions are met, the person often no longer wants the ex

real_case_outcomes.situation: Woman repeatedly used breakup threats and blocking as emotional regulation tools over 600+ days of a long-distance relationship; man gradually escalated from chasing to indifference to coldness
real_case_outcomes.decision: After man's final cold withdrawal, woman continued to press for in-person breakup conversation and sent messages over two days
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Man agreed to a 'goodbye dinner' but showed complete emotional withdrawal; relationship ended with man in a position of power and woman in reactive pursuit mode
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Using protest behavior (threatening to leave, blocking) as a reassurance-seeking mechanism depletes the partner's tolerance incrementally; by the time the person realizes the strategy has stopped working, the partner's emotional exit is already complete

real_case_outcomes.situation: Man in a two-year relationship had a one-night encounter during a home visit; the other party threatened to expose the infidelity unless paid 50,000 RMB; the current girlfriend was already told before the ultimatum was made; the couple chose to stay together
real_case_outcomes.decision: The girlfriend forgave the partner and continued the relationship; the offending partner attempted behavioral compliance (transparency, deleting ambiguous messages) but gradually began resenting the ongoing monitoring
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The betrayed partner's distrust continued to escalate rather than decrease; the offending partner shifted from self-blame to resentment ('I've tried, why won't she trust me?'); the relationship deteriorated and ended without resolution
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Forgiveness is not the same as trust restoration; staying together after infidelity requires an explicit ongoing repair process by both parties. The offending partner's inability to sustain tolerance of monitoring without resentment was the proximate cause of collapse — not the original infidelity

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person was in a relationship where the partner showed low reciprocal investment (no clear reciprocation, no commitment signals); person continued the relationship while experiencing insomnia, weight loss, and emotional instability
real_case_outcomes.decision: Continued the relationship despite clear somatic distress signals, rationalizing that one-sided effort was acceptable
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Relationship ended on extremely painful terms ('异常惨烈'); the commenter identifies that the body had been signaling the correct answer far earlier than the mind accepted it
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When somatic distress (insomnia, appetite disruption, emotional dysregulation) is chronic and tracks the relationship rather than external stressors, it is a reliable leading indicator that should be acted on — not overridden

real_case_outcomes.situation: Woman relocates to be with boyfriend, having explicitly stated that deception is her hard limit. Within the first year, discovers a suspicious contact. Boyfriend provides a minimizing explanation, refuses to delete contact, and deflects by suggesting she should change herself to resemble the other woman. Under continued pressure, he discloses layered truth: the woman was not a stranger but a multi-year friend concealed from the start, with instructions given to her to stay silent during girlfriend's visits.
real_case_outcomes.decision: After processing the full pattern — one year of sustained deception, coordinated third-party concealment, deflection of responsibility, and layered disclosure only under pressure — the poster decides to leave.
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Poster states she is preparing to leave and does not intend to see him again. The decision is framed as clear once the full pattern was visible.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When deception is structural (multi-year, coordinated, involving third-party management) rather than situational, and when the partner's response to discovery is deflection rather than accountability, the diagnostic question is not 'can trust be rebuilt?' but 'was the relationship ever operating on honest terms?' The answer in this case reframes the exit as a correction rather than a loss.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person owned their mistakes, apologized verbally and through changed behavior, and offered to support their partner's growth; partner admitted they didn't want to do the work of growth and moved to a new, 'easier' relationship
real_case_outcomes.decision: Person continued fighting for the relationship alone while partner was already checked out
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Partner left for someone who 'doesn't pressure him as much.' Person left processing having fought alone and been strung along.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When one partner is doing all the relational work and the other explicitly opts out of growth, the relationship is functionally over regardless of the willing partner's effort. Recognizing this earlier would prevent prolonged one-sided investment.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person waited 6 weeks before reaching out post-breakup and received no response; now at 3 months of silence, suspects ex has avoidant attachment
real_case_outcomes.decision: Reached out once at 6 weeks, then returned to silence
real_case_outcomes.outcome: No response after 3 months; person acknowledges there may be no hope
real_case_outcomes.lesson: A single outreach attempt after extended silence with no response, combined with avoidant attachment signals in the ex, is a strong indicator that further pursuit will not produce results; the 3-month silence window appears to be a community-recognized threshold

real_case_outcomes.situation: 20-year-old on second breakup, ended on mutual good terms but unwanted by her; partner cited incompatibility rather than fault
real_case_outcomes.decision: Post asks for help — still in early processing stage
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Not yet resolved in thread; surfaced as example of the specific difficulty of 'good terms' breakups where there is no anger to process and loss is ambiguous
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Amicable breakups create a distinct psychological challenge — the absence of wrongdoing removes the anger channel for grief, making loss harder to metabolize than acrimonious splits where anger provides processing energy

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person was left by a partner who stated they were emotionally unavailable and unable to reciprocate the love offered, framing the breakup as being 'for the other person's good'
real_case_outcomes.decision: Initial response was confusion and pain; the receiving partner questioned the authenticity of the relationship and the partner's prior expressions of love
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Community consensus framed this as a recognizable pattern — the leaving partner's stated reason (not being healed, unable to give love) is real but does not constitute an invitation to wait; the grief is valid but the relationship is over
real_case_outcomes.lesson: An emotionally generous exit framing ('you deserve better') should be heard as a complete ending, not a conditional one — the person leaving may genuinely mean it as kindness, but it functions as closure, not a promissory note

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person who stayed in a relationship through repeated lying and infidelity, depleting their self-worth in order to preserve the partnership
real_case_outcomes.decision: Tolerated the violations rather than leaving, continuing to invest in the relationship
real_case_outcomes.outcome: When the relationship ended (not on their terms), they were left with both the grief of loss and a depleted sense of self — describing themselves as having 'lost themselves' and now standing at a crossroads about whether a healthy relationship future was even possible for them
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Tolerating boundary violations to save a relationship does not save the relationship — it only ensures that when the ending comes, it arrives alongside an identity crisis. The cost of staying through betrayal is paid in full at the exit, not distributed across the relationship.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person who gave their all with clear boundaries across multiple relationships; partners consistently took them for granted and refused to respect the stated limits
real_case_outcomes.decision: Ended both relationships despite still having feelings for the partners
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Currently grieving but reorienting toward self-love as a foundation; acknowledges the pattern but has not yet resolved it
real_case_outcomes.lesson: High investment combined with clear boundaries does not protect against partners who simply will not respect those limits; the pattern of partner selection may need examination, not just the behavior within each relationship

real_case_outcomes.situation: Relationship ended because one partner wanted children and marriage; the other did not want children and was not ready for marriage
real_case_outcomes.decision: Ended the relationship to allow the partner who wanted those things to pursue them
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Described as painful but correct — staying would have led to resentment
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Incompatibility on foundational life goals (children, marriage) is not a problem that communication or love resolves — the honest move is separation before resentment accrues, not after

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person was ghosted by an avoidant partner for a year with no explanation
real_case_outcomes.decision: Waited; eventually the avoidant returned, declared love, went to therapy, reintroduced them to family, and took back painful statements
real_case_outcomes.outcome: They reconciled and continued for four years; the avoidant ended it again mid-argument in the same pattern as before; the dumpee this time did not chase, did not cry, and felt the relationship was simply expired rather than devastating
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Return plus genuine love plus therapy does not guarantee a different ending if the core conflict pattern is unchanged; however, the second ending can be experienced with significantly more peace if the dumpee has done their own work in the interim — the grief ceiling is lower the second time

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person who repeatedly attracted avoidant partners and ended things with secure ones, recognizing the pattern was rooted in childhood (fearful home environment where peace felt foreign)
real_case_outcomes.decision: Instead of focusing on the specific ex, did the inner work on childhood trauma — used dream analysis, therapy framing, and the concept of 'reparenting' the inner wounded child
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Developed a self-described 'adult' internal overseer that could observe and redirect thoughts calmly; framed this as a structural change rather than just healing from one breakup
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When the same attachment pattern repeats across multiple relationships, the work is not about the specific ex — it is about the internal system that keeps selecting and tolerating the same dynamic; healing at that level requires addressing the childhood origin, not just the surface breakup

real_case_outcomes.situation: Commenter in analogous situation: 2-year relationship ended because partner said she 'needed to find herself.' Found her on Hinge within 1-2 weeks; she was in a new relationship within a month.
real_case_outcomes.decision: Commenter reported being okay, having made new friends and hobbies.
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Recovery was achieved; commenter described being better off. The 'finding herself' reason was implicitly revealed as a cover story by the speed of her new relationship.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The 'I need to find myself' breakup reason, like religious or spiritual reasons, frequently functions as a socially acceptable cover for simply wanting to date someone else or return to single life — the timeline of the ex's next relationship is a reliable signal of the true reason.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person went 1.5 years no contact after a breakup that triggered deep depression; had been hoping the ex would change their mind and return
real_case_outcomes.decision: Accepted that the ex was not returning and continued no contact
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Reported gradual recovery of identity and emotional stability — 'every day I become more like myself'
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Acceptance of the finality of a breakup, even when painful, is a prerequisite for recovery — hope for return actively delays the recovery process

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person raised by grandparents after biological mother lost parental rights due to drugs and abuse before age 3; learned the truth in high school from a romantic partner; grandparents had died before the person could ask questions; biological parents found them via social media the same year
real_case_outcomes.decision: Re-established contact with biological parents, then went no contact again within a short period after seeing why grandparents had kept them away
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Spent early 20s in a different state to escape identity confusion; returned at 36 still processing how life would have differed with early disclosure; estranged from biological family
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When the protective generation (grandparents) dies before disclosure, the person has no safe anchor for processing the revelation — and biological family contact made without that anchor often reconfirms the original danger rather than providing resolution

real_case_outcomes.situation: Multiple commenters described their own past experiences of being in abusive relationships where they had to ghost or block friends to comply with a controlling partner's demands
real_case_outcomes.decision: They ghosted or blocked friends not out of personal rejection but to satisfy a controlling partner or to prevent the partner from seeing sympathetic communication
real_case_outcomes.outcome: After leaving the abusive relationship, those friends reported they had always noticed something was wrong with how the partner spoke to them — the 'I never liked how he spoke to her' observation was a real signal, not post-hoc rationalization
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Bystander discomfort with how a partner speaks to someone in front of others is a reliable early indicator of controlling dynamics — and it predicts exactly the kind of friend-management behavior seen in this case

real_case_outcomes.situation: Mother repeatedly disrespected adult child's husband and refused to change behavior despite being given chances
real_case_outcomes.decision: Adult child eventually went no-contact with mother
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The behavior never changed across multiple opportunities; NC became the only way to protect the marriage
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When a family member's disrespect of a partner is a sustained pattern and chances produce only promises without behavior change, escalating to NC is the predictable endpoint — acting earlier reduces cumulative harm

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person lost 60 lbs and observed the change in how men treated them before and after
real_case_outcomes.decision: Chose voluntary celibacy rather than continue engaging with a dating pool they found structurally disappointing
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Reports being happier; the pattern of treatment change was sufficiently distressing that exit from the system was preferable to continued navigation within it
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The differential in treatment before and after appearance change can be genuinely radicalizing — the experience of receiving appearance-conditional treatment is often only fully visible in contrast, and for some people the revelation changes their relationship with the dating market permanently

real_case_outcomes.situation: Cheater's sister initially hostile to OP, believing they had broken up 4 months prior based on what her brother told the family
real_case_outcomes.decision: OP answered the call, gave her side of the story including the timeline and the fabricated dead grandparents story, and sent Tinder receipts after hanging up
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Sister softened but revealed she had introduced the affair partner to the cheater herself; sister's primary concern shifted to the cheater also having a Tinder account while dating her friend — not to OP's welfare
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Engaging the cheater's family may produce new information about the deception's full scope, but their loyalty and concern will center on their own network, not on the betrayed partner; calibrate expectations accordingly

real_case_outcomes.situation: Person experiencing their own grief spiral had a partner who was burning out but remained indirect about their limits and intentions rather than stating them explicitly
real_case_outcomes.decision: Partner hid feelings and intentions, eventually left or withdrew without prior explicit communication
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The grieving person, already in a fog, sensed something was wrong, which worsened their burnout; when things ended or escalated, they had received no clear warning and spiraled more severely
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Indirect communication of limits by the healthy partner is not protective — it is harmful to both parties; explicit directness about needs and stakes, even when it feels cruel, produces better outcomes than gradual silent withdrawal

real_case_outcomes.situation: Commenter's ex-husband opened the relationship but became unable to cope when she began seeing someone and he had not found anyone
real_case_outcomes.decision: Couple entered couples therapy to manage his distress about her having a connection while he didn't
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The asymmetric distress revealed that his interest in polyamory was conditional on him having options — it was not a genuine lifestyle preference
real_case_outcomes.lesson: A partner's genuine comfort with polyamory is tested when the other partner actually finds someone, not during the abstract discussion phase; distress at that point is diagnostic

real_case_outcomes.situation: An OBGYN observed patients recovering from traumatic birth and post-partum surgeries over time
real_case_outcomes.decision: Tracked outcomes across patients with different home support environments
real_case_outcomes.outcome: She reported being able to predict which patients would heal successfully vs. which would deteriorate (eventually requiring hysterectomy) based primarily on home stress levels and quality of partner/family support — not just clinical variables
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Social and relational environment during medical recovery is a clinical variable, not just a quality-of-life factor. Staying in a high-conflict or emotionally draining relationship during cancer treatment or post-surgical recovery may have direct medical consequences beyond emotional suffering.

real_case_outcomes.situation: Same case: after two days of contact attempts post-breakup, the woman shifted to shared activity (playing games together) instead of emotional confrontation
real_case_outcomes.decision: Dropped the emotional pressure, engaged in low-stakes shared enjoyment
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Man spontaneously initiated affection and suggested reconciliation after the game session
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Shared enjoyment and low-pressure interaction can reactivate residual attachment faster than direct emotional appeal; the ex needs to re-experience positive feelings, not be argued into them
