reframing_moves.example_language: 'I say that I know what it's like to be in a marriage with someone who might love you but doesn't like you and it's worth not settling.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: He got upset when I brought up how I felt — maybe I said it wrong or the timing was bad
reframing_moves.reframe: His response to your expressed hurt is not feedback about your delivery — it is the most direct data you have about his capacity for repair
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Stops the person from optimizing their own communication style to manage an unmanageable dynamic; redirects attention from 'how can I say this better' to 'what does this response tell me about the relationship's ceiling'
reframing_moves.example_language: I have fallen for the old rope-a-dope MANY times — where they get all upset about me being upset, instead of issues getting fixed.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I should have broken up with him the 'right' way — in person, civilly
reframing_moves.reframe: Not giving him 'the chance or opportunity to manipulate me by taking the civil route' is not a failure of decency — it is recognition that civility with a manipulator is a trap, not a virtue
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It decouples the concept of being a good person from the method of exit — releases the moral obligation framing that controlling partners deliberately install to maintain access
reframing_moves.example_language: I really appreciate each person who gave me the strength and courage to end things on my terms and not give him the chance or opportunity to manipulate me by taking the civil route.

reframing_moves.original_framing: His behavior might be explained by his ex also having red hair — it must have struck a nerve
reframing_moves.reframe: Comment [25] and [26] together reframe this: even if the emotional cause is valid, the method of expression is what matters — 'adults communicate' the underlying feeling rather than issuing a control directive
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It separates the question of whether a feeling is understandable from whether a behavior is acceptable, preventing the OP (or reader) from using emotional context as a reason to excuse control
reframing_moves.example_language: Adults communicate, and say things like 'If you dye your hair red I'll think of my ex every time I see you' — not 'If you dye your hair I'll break up with you.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Is wanting to be seen and validated through your interests or appearance a sign of shallowness?
reframing_moves.reframe: Wanting validation for how you express yourself is universal — the question is whether the expression hurts others or yourself, not whether the category of expression is serious enough
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the hierarchy between 'serious' interests (hobbies, collectibles) and 'shallow' ones (fashion, material goods) by pointing to the shared psychological function underneath both
reframing_moves.example_language: Wanting to be seen or validated is human, not something exclusive to one type of interest

reframing_moves.original_framing: We have so many problems but things will get better once [external condition] changes
reframing_moves.reframe: External conditions changed — distance ended, employment stabilized — and the relationship still failed; the problems were never about the external conditions
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Uses the poster's own lived outcome as proof that the 'wait for conditions to improve' frame was a deferral mechanism, not a diagnosis — makes the pattern legible in retrospect so others can recognize it prospectively
reframing_moves.example_language: 好不容易结束异地，他也有了一份稳定的工作，但是以前的问题堆积一直没解决，最终谈不下去了 — 'We finally ended the long distance, he had a stable job, but the old problems had piled up and were never resolved, and in the end it couldn't continue'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'They broke up with me, so I must not be good enough — I need to fix myself to win them back'
reframing_moves.reframe: The breakup is their action, not your verdict — the question of whether you are 'enough' is separate from the question of whether they chose to leave
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Decouples self-worth from the ex's decision; prevents the person from taking on disproportionate self-blame that distorts the diagnostic process and creates an unhealthy power dynamic where all change obligations fall on one side
reframing_moves.example_language: '他说分手，和，你不够好，这两件事，为什么要画等号？'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I've been trying so hard and doing everything right, why won't they respond?'
reframing_moves.reframe: You're giving what you think they should want, not what they actually need. The effort is real but the target is wrong.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Breaks the assumption that intensity of effort equals quality of approach; opens the person to reassessing whether their reconciliation actions match the ex's actual emotional needs
reframing_moves.example_language: '很多人在挽回过程中总是做一些感动自己的行为……你给的不一定是他想要的。'

reframing_moves.original_framing: My partner has so many flaws — bad temper, always gaming, never initiates contact — maybe we're not right for each other
reframing_moves.reframe: These are part of who they are — you chose this person; the question is whether you can accept who they fundamentally are, not whether they are flawed
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Redirects from evaluating the partner against an ideal standard to evaluating the person's own choice and acceptance capacity — prevents the cognitive trap of using ordinary human imperfection as a justification for exit when the real issue is unaddressed attraction loss
reframing_moves.example_language: 这都是他的一部分啊 — 'These are all part of who he is'

reframing_moves.original_framing: The offending partner frames their situation as 'I've been working hard to rebuild trust but my partner still won't trust me — what else can I do?'
reframing_moves.reframe: Comment [rank=2] implicitly reframes this: the partner who breaks trust loses the right to set the timeline for its restoration. The question is not 'what more can I do' but 'can I sustain the required consistency long enough for the betrayed partner's system to recalibrate?'
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the transactional framing (effort for forgiveness) and replaces it with a time-and-consistency framing — which is actually how trust psychology works
reframing_moves.example_language: '信任是情侣之间的一层保护层，但是它却像泡泡一样，一戳就会破，再怎么补都补不起来' ('Trust is like a bubble — once popped, patching it is insufficient; you need to rebuild the whole layer')

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I don't feel the same way I used to — does that mean I've fallen out of love?'
reframing_moves.reframe: Happiness in a long relationship is like air — you don't feel it while it's there; you only notice it when it's gone. The question is not whether excitement is present but whether you would feel loss if the relationship ended.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the evaluation criterion from the presence of a positive signal (excitement) to the response to a hypothetical negative event (loss), which is a more reliable measure of genuine attachment
reframing_moves.example_language: 幸福很多时候就像空气，人身处幸福的时候往往感受不到幸福的存在，直到失去的时候才会意识到 (Happiness is often like air — you don't feel it while you have it, only when it's gone)

reframing_moves.original_framing: Treating the question as 'is this serious enough to end the relationship over?'
reframing_moves.reframe: Reframe to: 'What does the pattern of behavior — not the content of any single lie, but the duration, the coordination, the deflection, and the staged disclosure — predict about future behavior under similar conditions of conflict of interest?'
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Moves the analysis from incident-level (was this one lie bad enough?) to pattern-level (does this behavioral pattern predict trustworthy partnership going forward?). Pattern-level analysis is more predictive and less susceptible to minimization.
reframing_moves.example_language: '为何你们既然没有问题，怎么你做的事都不得不让人怀疑心里有鬼？' — the poster is intuitively reaching for pattern-level analysis: if the facts are innocent, why does the behavior architecture look like concealment?
reframing_moves._source: zhihu_被男友欺骗后怎想重新建立信任.txt

reframing_moves.original_framing: I lost a good person — bad luck, bad timing
reframing_moves.reframe: You didn't lose her — you failed someone who genuinely loved you. Loss implies something happened to you; failure means you had agency and didn't use it.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: The framing shift from passive loss to active failure is uncomfortable but accurate, and it's the only framing that makes change possible. Passive loss framing produces grief without accountability; failure framing produces accountability that can drive change.
reframing_moves.example_language: I didn't lose a 'good girl.' I failed someone who genuinely loved me.

reframing_moves.original_framing: They broke up with me but I know this relationship is worth saving — how do I convince them?
reframing_moves.reframe: You cannot fight for someone who has already made a decision; the only move available to the dumpee is to demonstrate they are okay without the ex, not to persuade
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Dissolves the illusion that persuasion or demonstration of love is a viable lever when you are the dumpee; replaces a losing strategy with one that at minimum protects self-worth
reframing_moves.example_language: If you've been dumped, you cannot fight. It really is that cut and dry.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I relapsed and texted them — I ruined all my progress
reframing_moves.reframe: Every time you relapse and regret it, your mind overwrites its memory of this person as safe. It is a withdrawal symptom, not a reset.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Recontextualizes relapse as mechanistically useful data rather than failure; removes the shame layer and reactivates willingness to continue
reframing_moves.example_language: Your head is battling a withdrawal. They were your drug.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I want them back
reframing_moves.reframe: You don't really want them back — the version of them that you loved no longer exists because they no longer love you; what you want is the feeling back
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Separates the target of desire (the person as they were) from the actual accessible object (the feeling, which can be recovered through other means), making continued pursuit of the ex logically incoherent rather than just emotionally difficult
reframing_moves.example_language: You don't really want them back. The version of them that you loved doesn't exist anymore because they don't love you anymore. You want the old them back — you want the feeling back.

reframing_moves.original_framing: My partner said I deserve someone who can give me everything I give — but they can't do that right now because they're not healed. I'm waiting for them.
reframing_moves.reframe: The person you thought they were — someone who would work through difficulty with you — wouldn't have exited instead of healing with you. The exit itself is the data.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Redirects attention from the partner's stated reasons (which are future-oriented and ambiguous) to their actual behavior (which is present and concrete) — breaks the waiting posture by identifying that the hoped-for version of the partner and the version who actually left are inconsistent with each other
reframing_moves.example_language: 'The person you thought they were wouldn't have given up on us like they did'

reframing_moves.original_framing: I'm struggling to believe I'll ever love again or find someone better
reframing_moves.reframe: There are millions of people who said exactly this and found the love of their life — your disbelief right now is a symptom of where you are, not a prediction of where you'll end up
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Introduces base rate evidence to counter the person's individual-level catastrophizing — shifts from 'what I feel must be true' to 'what I feel is a known and temporary stage that many people have passed through'
reframing_moves.example_language: There's also millions of us that made it out and found the love of their life. I'm remaining hopeful on that for my sake as well.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I should start dating again quickly to feel better and move on
reframing_moves.reframe: Jumping into a rebound is like quitting a job you hated and signing a new contract the next day — reset means stop, think, rebuild
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Externalizes the dynamic through an analogy that makes the irrationality visible; the 'reset' frame creates a legitimate reason to pause that does not require the person to admit fear or inability
reframing_moves.example_language: That's like quitting a job you hated and signing a new contract the next day

reframing_moves.original_framing: Never invite someone into your life if you don't have the space for them
reframing_moves.reframe: Readiness is a precondition for starting, not just a nice-to-have — entering a relationship without genuine capacity is not a neutral act, it affects someone else's future
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It shifts the ethical weight of unreadiness from a private internal state to an interpersonal responsibility, making the decision to wait or step back feel principled rather than avoidant
reframing_moves.example_language: 'If you're not ready to step up to the plate, take your hands off another person's future.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: She said it was because of my jealousy, so I fixed my jealousy — now it should work
reframing_moves.reframe: She left you for someone else. You can always tell when it's 'because of your jealousy about my guy friends.' The jealousy was real, but it may have been the exit excuse, not the exit cause.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It forces the person to distinguish between the stated reason and the actual reason, which changes the risk assessment of reconciliation entirely — preventing them from building false confidence on a solved problem that was never the real problem
reframing_moves.example_language: I wouldn't put my trust in her 100% — I don't want to sugar coat it, there's always that huge possibility.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I miss them so much, I must still love them and maybe I made a mistake leaving / accepting it
reframing_moves.reframe: You are not experiencing love right now — you are experiencing withdrawal; your brain is not showing you an accurate picture of the relationship
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Introduces a physiological frame that removes moral weight from the feeling — it is not a signal about what you should do, it is a neurochemical process that will pass
reframing_moves.example_language: 'You are withdrawing from a person the same way an alcoholic is withdrawing from their vice, and during these moments your brain does not remember the bad and amplifies the good.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: They seem fine and have moved on — they must not have loved me as much as I loved them
reframing_moves.reframe: Your races are independent — their speed says nothing about your worth or about how much you were loved
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Severs the implicit comparison by introducing a different metaphor entirely (parallel marathons rather than a single race) — makes the ex's apparent recovery irrelevant to the person's own healing progress
reframing_moves.example_language: You run your own marathon at your own pace

reframing_moves.original_framing: I need to ask him what really happened so I can understand and move on
reframing_moves.reframe: Asking is pointless — his Bumble profile already told you the real reason. Closure comes from accepting what his actions revealed, not from what his words might say next.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Redirects the search for meaning from the unreliable source (the ex's future statements) to the already-available evidence (his post-breakup behavior), collapsing the justification for re-establishing contact
reframing_moves.example_language: "It's really pointless — better to ignore and forget few things for peace of mind and your future"

reframing_moves.original_framing: Communication problems in our relationship were about skill or effort — if we just talked more it would have worked
reframing_moves.reframe: Humans have the most advanced communication system of any animal on earth and we are still absolutely terrible at using it in relationships — this is a near-universal structural failure, not a personal one
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Normalizes the communication breakdown without excusing it, and shifts the user from self-blame or partner-blame toward a systemic understanding — which is more accurate and less paralyzing
reframing_moves.example_language: We have learned and created through evolution the most advanced form of communication amongst all animals on earth and yet we are still absolutely shite at using this to our advantage specifically in relationships.

reframing_moves.original_framing: My grandparents/parents kept this secret from me — should I be angry?
reframing_moves.reframe: The more useful question is not whether anger is justified, but what they were afraid of — understanding their fear makes the deception more navigable without requiring you to either condemn or excuse them
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Replaces a moral verdict question (should I be angry?) with a contextual understanding question — reduces the binary of forgiveness vs. betrayal and opens space for complex feeling
reframing_moves.example_language: They always planned on telling me but the way my sister treated me gave them pause — they were afraid of exactly what happened

reframing_moves.original_framing: Should I tell my girlfriend I saw the messages?
reframing_moves.reframe: The question is not whether to tell her — it is how to tell her in a way that makes her feel safe rather than more burdened
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts from a binary disclosure question to a delivery and framing question; assumes disclosure as the correct path and focuses energy on execution
reframing_moves.example_language: Let her know it was by accident that you saw it, but you are glad you did — and that she doesn't need to shield you from your own mother

reframing_moves.original_framing: He's been texting me nonstop to calm down and come home and talk — maybe I should hear him out.
reframing_moves.reframe: A person who committed this act and whose first response to your distress was to smile does not get a conversation. Minimum contact is a safety measure, not a cruelty.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reframes cutting off contact from an emotionally difficult choice (seeming 'cold' or 'unfair') to a logical protective measure, removing the guilt around not engaging.
reframing_moves.example_language: 'He doesn't even deserve to be told what is happening with the pregnancy. I'd get an attorney and stop all contact. He can go through a lawyer if he wants info.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: He was acting loving and cuddly — doesn't that mean he meant well?
reframing_moves.reframe: Acting loving while waiting for the police to arrive is not evidence of good intent — it mirrors a specific documented control tactic where the abuser destabilizes you and then positions themselves as the calm, caring one
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Breaks the binary model of 'loving = safe' by providing a mechanism through which affection and harm can coexist intentionally, changing the meaning of the affectionate behavior
reframing_moves.example_language: That he's trying to brush it off and was acting loving and cuddly waiting for the cops to show up is seriously concerning and mirrors abusive control tactics I've personally witnessed on more than one occasion.

reframing_moves.original_framing: He's a great guy and we're happy — I don't want to lose the relationship over one small thing
reframing_moves.reframe: This isn't about the past you. This is about the future you — what happens when you're pregnant, or injured, or 50?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the temporal frame from the current-state relationship (which is positive) to the future-state relationship (which is uncertain given this new data) — makes the stakes legible in terms of long-term risk rather than current loss
reframing_moves.example_language: None of us stay at peak beauty for more than a few years. Before too long, OP like everyone else will have wrinkles, saggy skin, might get stressed at work and gain a few pounds

reframing_moves.original_framing: I sound like a whiny baby for describing all this
reframing_moves.reframe: Commenters reframed it as: the impulse to minimize and apologize is a symptom of the abuse, not an accurate self-assessment — you are not whining, you are describing a crime
reframing_moves.why_it_works: The self-minimization frame keeps the victim complicit in erasing the severity of what happened; the reframe externalizes the minimization as the abuser's installed behavior, restoring the victim's right to name their experience accurately
reframing_moves.example_language: 'You are not a whiner or complainer, you weren't [wrong for] verbalizing your trauma and it was completely justified.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: OP focused on the content of the cheater's email ('he said I love you')
reframing_moves.reframe: Community implicitly reframed by noting the absence of apology as the signal: the email asked to talk and closed with affection but contained no acknowledgment of wrongdoing
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Moves the evaluative lens from what was said (affection, request to talk) to what was absent (apology, accountability) — teaches the reader to read absence as information
reframing_moves.example_language: 'No, he did not apologize for anything. He ended the email with I love you.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Therapy might help — you should think about couples counseling or waiting to see if she gets better
reframing_moves.reframe: The grief you need to process is not about the marriage ending but about mourning the person your partner used to be — that requires grief-specialized individual therapy, not couples work
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Separates two distinct psychological tasks (processing the loss of the old partner vs. repairing the current relationship) and identifies the appropriate intervention for the one that is actually actionable
reframing_moves.example_language: You're also grieving the person your wife used to be — it's hard to accept that the person you fell in love with no longer exists

reframing_moves.original_framing: What should I do? I don't know how much longer I can do this
reframing_moves.reframe: You are under no obligation to stay. You are not married. You can decide how long you are willing to wait — but the decision is yours to make, not a moral test you are failing
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Restores agency to a person who has framed themselves as trapped by love and loyalty; names that the relationship has not yet crossed the legal and formal threshold of marriage, which changes the stakes of leaving
reframing_moves.example_language: 'You are under absolutely no obligation to. You're not married. You're free to go anytime'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Maybe it really was just weed and a Switch, in which case maybe I overreacted
reframing_moves.reframe: Even if it turns out what he's hiding isn't as gruesome as our imaginations, her husband's behavior remains seriously problematic — the gaslighting and the locked room are the issue regardless of contents
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Decouples the evaluation of the partner's behavior from the evaluation of the secret's content; prevents the innocent-contents reveal from functioning as behavioral exoneration
reframing_moves.example_language: Her husband's behavior remains seriously problematic — this is textbook gaslighting

reframing_moves.original_framing: Relationships and marriages require constant hard work — we're doing the work by being in counseling
reframing_moves.reframe: A relationship that requires constant effortful struggle is not the same as one that occasionally requires work. The baseline should be ease, trust, and support — not a continuous hole you need therapy to keep climbing out of.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It challenges a widely held cultural script ('marriage is hard work') that normalizes chronic relationship dysfunction; resets the reference point from 'are we working on it' to 'what should this feel like'
reframing_moves.example_language: Despite what feels like decades of societal conditioning proclaiming that marriage is hard work, relationships and marriages are not supposed to be difficult and should not take constant effort.

reframing_moves.original_framing: He's polyamorous and says he can't do poly with limits — is that true?
reframing_moves.reframe: Ethical non-monogamy is entirely built on negotiated agreements. 'I can't do poly with limits' is not a description of polyamory — it is a description of wanting to do whatever he wants with no accountability. Those are not the same thing.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Separates the legitimate practice from the self-serving redefinition the husband deployed — OP had been accepting his definition as authoritative
reframing_moves.example_language: Comment [34]: 'how little research these men do, and how much they weaponized therapy speak to devalue their spouses just to excuse their own cheating'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Should I sell the extra car while we're still married?
reframing_moves.reframe: She'd get less out of it this way. If there is only one car, it should go to OP since her mother bought it.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reframes the car question from 'what's fair right now' to 'what preserves OP's legal and financial position at divorce' — introduces the time horizon of separation into a decision being made in the present tense
reframing_moves.example_language: She'd get less out of it this way... it should go to OP since her mother bought it.

reframing_moves.original_framing: He kept backtracking on his threat, calling it a joke and trying to continue the conversation
reframing_moves.reframe: Comment [23] reframes what the OP is allowed to be simultaneously: 'You can be a good person with strong boundaries who won't put up with people treating them with such disregard' — the reframe dissolves the implied conflict between being kind and holding a limit
reframing_moves.why_it_works: People with empathy-based identities often experience boundary-holding as a contradiction of their self-concept; naming the compatibility directly removes that internal barrier to action
reframing_moves.example_language: You can be a good person with strong boundaries who won't put up with people treating them with such disregard.

reframing_moves.original_framing: This sub defaults to 'break up' for anything that doesn't resolve instantly
reframing_moves.reframe: The advice quality depends on what information you give — when you demonstrate that real communication capacity exists, informed commenters update their assessment away from the default breakup recommendation
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reminds advice-seekers that community default recommendations are heuristics for the average case, not determinations for their specific situation — quality of communication evidence changes the recommendation
reframing_moves.example_language: If this weren't the case, I would have gone to the typical Reddit default of: you aren't compatible, breakup, don't even try

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I need to get them back quickly before they move on / start dating someone else'
reframing_moves.reframe: Urgency is an emotion, not a real deadline — the ex going on dates does not close the window; the relevant variable is your state when you re-engage, not how fast you re-engage
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Defuses the panic that drives clinging and premature re-contact; reorients the person toward the only variable they can actually control (their own condition) rather than the variable they cannot (the ex's timeline)
reframing_moves.example_language: '急什么呢？相个亲而已，真能成吗？成了就能不分手吗？不分手就能结婚吗？时间那么长呢，啥事儿不能发生'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'Should I do no-contact to make them miss me?'
reframing_moves.reframe: No-contact is not a manipulation tactic to induce missing — it's a diagnostic and reset tool. The question is: what severity of breakup are you in, and what does the other person need to feel before contact can be productive?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the gamification mindset ('make them miss me') and replaces it with a calibration mindset that is responsive to the actual state of the relationship
reframing_moves.example_language: '断联时间太短的话，对方的负面情绪还没有得到缓解；太长的话，对方可能会彻底放下你。'
reframing_moves._source: zhihu_分手后还有挽回的可能吗.txt

reframing_moves.original_framing: I feel hurt and suspicious — something must be wrong, all suspicions are true
reframing_moves.reframe: Your feelings are real, but the question of whether your partner has actually done something wrong is separate from the question of whether you are in pain — conflating the two leads to acting on emotion as if it were evidence
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Introduces the distinction between emotional signal and factual claim — prevents impulsive exits driven by attachment anxiety while also not dismissing the possibility of genuine partner failure
reframing_moves.example_language: 所有的离开都是有征兆的，所有的怀疑都是真的 — this community aphorism ('all suspicions are true') is the framing being challenged; the reframe asks: true about your feelings, or true about your partner's actions?

reframing_moves.original_framing: User describes a cold, emotionally unavailable partner as 'not caring' or 'not loving enough'
reframing_moves.reframe: The top answer reframes avoidant coldness as a self-protective strategy, not an absence of feeling: the avoidant person does care, but has learned that showing care produces no return — so they mask it. The partner is not less loving; they are more defended
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Converts a judgment about the partner's character into an understanding of their history — opens space for the user to approach the partner with curiosity rather than grievance
reframing_moves.example_language: '你的他真的不在意吗？不，他是在意的。只不过，他不相信当自己做出的任何举动会真的有效' ('Does he really not care? No, he does care. He simply doesn't believe any action he takes will be effective')

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'The new option seems better than my current partner'
reframing_moves.reframe: You are comparing your current partner's fully-known reality against the new option's unknown surface. Apply the same nine questions to the new option that you would apply to your current partner.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Equalizes the comparison by making the asymmetry explicit; the new option only appears better because it has not been tested under the same conditions
reframing_moves.example_language: 目前伴侣有的缺点，新选择就一定不存在么？(Are you certain the new option doesn't have the same flaws as your current partner?)

reframing_moves.original_framing: How could they move on so fast? Did I ever mean anything to them?
reframing_moves.reframe: You won't know whether they're healing or simply avoiding. You can't know how they feel from what you see. And none of it matters — all you can control is how you deal with it.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Closes the epistemically invalid inference chain (visible behavior → true internal state → your worth) and redirects to the only variable the person can actually affect
reframing_moves.example_language: You won't know whether they're healing or simply avoiding. None of it matters.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I haven't made any progress; I still feel terrible
reframing_moves.reframe: The days passing is progress; you caring for yourself and trying your best is progress — progress is not measured by the absence of pain on a given day
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Decouples recovery progress from daily emotional state, preventing the common failure mode of interpreting a bad day as evidence that healing is not occurring
reframing_moves.example_language: The days passing is progress. You caring for yourself and trying your best is progress.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I keep forcing myself to hold on because we made so many commitments — promise rings, future plans — I can't just let that go.
reframing_moves.reframe: Forcing something that both people no longer want is working against the flow — and life smooths out when you stop.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reframes release not as giving up or accepting defeat but as alignment with reality — removes the sunk cost framing ('I've invested too much to leave') by introducing a forward-looking ease narrative ('things get better when you stop resisting')
reframing_moves.example_language: 'I just know that I'm no longer going to try to force or hold onto something that clearly both people don't want. It's working against the flow — I have to try to go with the flow. Life smooths out when I do that.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: I don't understand how I ended up with an avoidant — I thought he was secure, so I can't tell anymore
reframing_moves.reframe: You didn't mess up — this is exactly how you tell. Your relationship faces an extreme stressor and your attachment styles come out. It takes that one rupture to push them into their full potential as avoidant
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes self-blame by converting perceived personal failure into a systemic insight; reframes the inability to detect early as normal rather than as negligence
reframing_moves.example_language: You didn't mess up. This is exactly how you tell.

reframing_moves.original_framing: How do I get them to realize what they lost / prove I was worth it
reframing_moves.reframe: You are already worth it regardless of whether they realize it — the goal is not to prove worth to them but to remove unhealthy attachment for yourself
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Decouples self-worth from the ex's recognition, eliminating the dependency that makes the person's healing contingent on the ex's behavior
reframing_moves.example_language: 'You are worth it regardless, and the best revenge is to be happy without them.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: I keep having dreams about them — no contact isn't working
reframing_moves.reframe: No contact doesn't reach your subconscious yet — dreams are withdrawal symptoms, not signals; your conscious mind is detoxing and your subconscious is catching up
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Separates the domain of voluntary behavior (no contact) from involuntary neurological processing (dreams), removing the guilt and confusion that comes from treating dreams as behavioral failures — also normalizes the experience as temporary and physiological
reframing_moves.example_language: The dreams are the only place where no contact doesn't work yet

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I still have such strong feelings for them — that must mean they are irreplaceable'
reframing_moves.reframe: Your memory of them is not the same as them — each time you recall someone in distress, you partially reconstruct the memory; the person you are suffering over is partly your own construction, not the real person
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Introduces cognitive distance between the felt experience and the object of the experience; gives the person a framework to hold their feelings seriously while not treating them as objective evidence about the ex's worth
reframing_moves.example_language: '我们每从大脑中提取关于他的回忆一次，就重构一次……失恋时，我们大脑中的他，根本不是现实中的他'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I'm improving myself so they'll see how much I've changed and come back'
reframing_moves.reframe: Do it for yourself, not for them. If your motivation is their response, you'll become resentful when they don't reward the effort — and they'll smell the performance.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Decouples self-improvement from the ex's validation, making it sustainable regardless of reconciliation outcome, and more credible when observed
reframing_moves.example_language: '当你抱着为自己改变的目的，会发现轻松很多……最终的受益人还是你自己，对方并没有得到你的任何好处。'

reframing_moves.original_framing: User asks whether to 'repair' the protective layer of trust that has been damaged
reframing_moves.reframe: Comment [rank=2] reframes repair vs. rebuild: rather than patching the damaged trust layer, the approach must be to construct a new one from scratch — because patched trust is structurally weaker than rebuilt trust
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reduces the psychological burden of trying to restore an exact prior state (impossible) and reorients the effort toward building something new (possible) — reduces the 'we can never go back' grief response
reframing_moves.example_language: '与其去修修补补，不如重新建立这个保护层' ('Rather than patching and mending, rebuild the protective layer from scratch')

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I should push through the pain because giving up is weak'
reframing_moves.reframe: Your body is the most honest reporter you have. If you are sleeping badly, eating badly, and crying regularly, your body has already answered the question — the question is whether you are willing to listen.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Bypasses the cognitive rationalization loop by elevating somatic data to epistemic authority; reframes listening to your body not as weakness but as honesty
reframing_moves.example_language: 感情好不好，身体都知道。你的身体是感情的最佳晴雨表 (Whether a relationship is good, your body knows. Your body is the best barometer of your feelings)

reframing_moves.original_framing: I need to get closure by talking to them
reframing_moves.reframe: You're deeply vulnerable right now. If you want closure, wait until the pain is no longer acute and you can think more clearly.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Separates the legitimate need for closure from the timing of seeking it; validates the goal while protecting the person from the predictable consequences of pursuing it while impaired
reframing_moves.example_language: Keep in mind you're deeply vulnerable right now. You will say things you'll regret later.

reframing_moves.original_framing: They said horrible things about me that aren't true — how do I make people see the real story
reframing_moves.reframe: They are rewriting history to cope with their own guilt — this is about their psychology, not an accurate account of you
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the person from a defensive posture (trying to correct the record) and places the narrative distortion back onto the ex as their burden to manage
reframing_moves.example_language: 'It's their way of coping with the guilt, they rewrite the history making you the bad person so they feel justified in leaving you.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Healing is getting better every day — but today was worse than yesterday, so something is wrong
reframing_moves.reframe: Healing is like the S&P 500 — short-term crashes don't change the long-term upward trend; trust the trend, not the daily fluctuation
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Replaces a linear model of healing (which produces catastrophizing on bad days) with a volatility model (which normalizes bad days as expected noise within a positive trajectory) — reduces the risk of breaking no contact on a bad day out of despair
reframing_moves.example_language: Trust the trend, not the daily fluctuation

reframing_moves.original_framing: I miss who I was when I was with them — I feel empty now, like I'm nothing
reframing_moves.reframe: You might miss not just them but who you were with them. Your brain is recalibrating your identity. Feeling empty doesn't mean you're nothing — you're just recharging the battery.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Separates grief for the person from grief for a version of the self; names the identity-recalibration process explicitly, which converts existential emptiness into a temporary and functional state
reframing_moves.example_language: Feeling empty doesn't mean you're nothing, you're just recharging the battery.
